extracted.intended_audience: People asking questions on Mathematics Stack Exchange (prospective and new site users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing acceptable, answerable math questions on Mathematics Stack Exchange: what to avoid, how to scope questions, and when subjective topics are permitted. Focus is on producing practical, well-scoped, non-discussion questions appropriate for the main site.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-topic for this site
rubrics_metrics.description: First, make sure that your question is on-topic for this site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link to and consult the site's on-topic guidance; questions not about mathematics (as defined by the site) are inappropriate for the main Q&A and may be closed or migrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, answerable questions based on actual problems
rubrics_metrics.description: You should only ask practical, answerable questions based on actual problems that you face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid chatty, open-ended questions. Questions must be concrete problems that can be answered; hypothetical, overly broad, or purely conversational prompts are discouraged because they diminish usefulness and push other questions off the front page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably scoped / not book-length
rubrics_metrics.description: Your questions should be reasonably scoped. If you can imagine an entire book that answers your question, you’re asking too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope questions so they can be answered in a focused post; extremely broad survey or textbook-sized requests are off-topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation: not for discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: If your motivation for asking the question is 'I would like to participate in a discussion about ______', then you should not be asking here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your motivation is 'I would like others to explain ______ to me', then you are probably OK. Site discussion-type content belongs in Chat or on Meta (for site-related issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questions where every answer is equally valid (non-constructive subjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asking subjective questions where every answer is equally valid: 'What’s your favorite ______?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-constructive subjective questions generate opinion lists rather than explanations and are likely to be flagged or closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'your answer is provided along with the question' pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid questions where your answer is provided along with the question, and you expect more answers: 'I use ______ for ______, what do you use?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such formats solicit personal lists or polls rather than focused, expert answers and are inappropriate for the Q&A format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questions with no actual problem to be solved
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid questions where there is no actual problem to be solved: 'I’m curious if other people feel like I do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should present a clear problem, confusion, or task; pure curiosity about others' feelings/opinions is off-topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid open-ended, hypothetical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asking open-ended, hypothetical questions: 'What if ______ happened?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheticals without a concrete problem context invite speculation and are not a good fit for the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rants disguised as questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid questions that are just a rant in disguise: '______ sucks, am I right?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rants are not requests for help or explanation and will be closed or deleted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: inspire explanations of why and how
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions should inspire answers that explain 'why' and 'how'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good subjective questions require reasoned explanations, not one-line opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: encourage longer, detailed answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions tend to have long, not short, answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and encourage thorough, well-explained responses rather than brief preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: constructive, fair, impartial tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions have a constructive, fair, and impartial tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leading, loaded, or biased phrasing; present the issue neutrally to solicit useful answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: invite experiences over mere opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions invite sharing experiences over opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame questions so answerers can draw on concrete experience, examples, or practice rather than unsupported preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: require opinions backed by facts and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions insist that opinion be backed up with facts and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers should be evidence-based where possible, citing sources or explaining reasoning rather than asserting unsupported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive subjective: more than mindless social fun
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive subjective questions are more than just mindless social fun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should have lasting value to future readers, not just immediate entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site-related questions belong on Meta
rubrics_metrics.description: If your question is about the site itself, please don't ask it here. Visit our Meta site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Meta for discussions about what questions are appropriate, tag usage, feature requests, bugs, or site policy; the main site is for mathematics questions only.
